lessonRef.title: Concept model A: orienting the reader: situation, narrator, and characters

studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops orienting the reader: situation, narrator, and characters within the unit “Narrative Craft, Comparison, and the Year-End Portfolio.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's concept model a work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
The maple sap bucket held four gallons when it was full, which was thirty-two pounds, which was more than Dev could carry level.

He had asked for the job. That was the part he kept returning to as he shuffled down the slope with the bucket banging against his shin and sap slopping over the rim in bright cold splashes.

His older sister Anita carried two buckets and did not slop.

"You are fighting it," she said, without turning around.

"I am carrying it."

"You are fighting it. Watch." She stopped and set both buckets down in the snow. "Hold it away from your leg. Let your arm hang straight. Do not try to keep it still."

"If I do not keep it still it will spill."

"It spills because you keep stopping it."

That made no sense at all, so Dev tried it out of irritation. He let his arm go loose. The bucket swung forward, back, forward, in time with his steps, and the sap inside rocked and rode the swing instead of climbing the sides.

He walked forty feet without spilling a drop.

"Huh," he said.

Anita picked up her buckets. "Dad taught me that. Grandpa taught him. Nobody figured it out. Somebody just says it to you and then you know it."

They emptied into the collection tank at the bottom of the hill, and Dev's arms were shaking, and the sap ran out of the bucket in a long amber rope that steamed slightly in the cold.

On the walk back up he thought about the fact that the trick was three sentences long. Three sentences, and a hundred years of people saying them to each other on this hill, and without them he would have carried buckets badly for the rest of his life and called it being tired.

He was still tired. But he was not fighting it anymore.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Weight of the Bucket”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what orienting the reader: situation, narrator, and characters asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Weight of the Bucket,” then answer: Trace how one example in the reading demonstrates orienting the reader: situation, narrator, and characters. Which step in the example does the most work?

Deliverable: Grade 4: a labeled explanation of the example and its most important step; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If orienting the reader: situation, narrator, and characters is not yet secure, return to “The Weight of the Bucket” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply orienting the reader: situation, narrator, and characters to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Weight of the Bucket.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
